title: t-SNE — Visualising High-Dimensional Data

blocks.t: From the notes
t-SNE, as written
t-SNE — t-distributed Stochastic Neighbour Embedding.

It is a non-linear dimensionality reduction technique used mainly for
visualisation — bringing very high-dimensional data down to
2D or 3D so we can plot it.

PCA is linear and tries to keep the global structure
(variance). t-SNE is non-linear and tries to keep the local
structure — points that were neighbours in high dimensions stay neighbours
in the plot.

Main parameter: perplexity (roughly, how many neighbours each point
should consider). Typical values 5 to 50.
It is used for visualisation, not as a feature-engineering step.

blocks.cap:
The 1797 handwritten digits of load_digits, 64 dimensions
reduced to 2. PCA leaves the classes tangled; t-SNE separates all ten. The two
methods optimise genuinely different things.

blocks.t: The algorithm
Step 1 — distances become probabilities in high-D

For each point $i$ define a Gaussian centred on it and convert distances into
conditional probabilities — "the probability that $i$ would pick $j$ as its
neighbour":

Note that the bandwidth $\sigma_i$ is different for every point. It is
chosen by binary search so that the entropy of $P_i$ hits a target set by the
user:

\operatorname{Perp}(P_i) = 2^{H(P_i)},
\qquad H(P_i)=-\sum_j p_{j|i}\log_2 p_{j|i} .

Perplexity is a smooth measure of the effective number of neighbours.
A point in a dense region gets a small $\sigma_i$; one in a sparse region gets a
large one. This adaptive bandwidth is why t-SNE copes with varying density where
DBSCAN's single global $\epsilon$ cannot.

Finally symmetrise, so that the pairwise affinities form a proper joint
distribution:
p_{ij}=\frac{p_{j|i}+p_{i|j}}{2n}.
Step 2 — probabilities in the 2-D map

In the low-dimensional map, use a Student-t distribution with one
degree of freedom (a Cauchy) instead of a Gaussian:
The crowding problem, and why the t-distribution fixes it

In $d$ dimensions the volume of a ball grows as $r^d$, so a point can have a
huge number of neighbours at moderate distance. In 2-D there is simply not
enough room to place them all at that distance — the moderately-distant
points get crushed towards the centre, and all structure collapses. This is the
crowding problem.

The Student-t has much heavier tails than a Gaussian. To achieve the same
$q_{ij}$ as a Gaussian would give at a moderate distance, the map must place the
pair further apart. The heavy tail therefore creates the extra room
needed, pushing dissimilar points out and letting clusters separate cleanly —
which is exactly the visual signature of a t-SNE plot.

It also has a computational benefit: $(1+\|y_i-y_j\|^2)^{-1}$ has no exponential,
so gradients are cheaper and better behaved than in the original SNE.

blocks.t: Step 3 — match the two distributions

Minimise the Kullback–Leibler divergence between $P$ and $Q$ over the map
coordinates $y$:
\boxed{ C = \mathrm{KL}(P \| Q) = \sum_{i \ne j} p_{ij} \log\frac{p_{ij}}{q_{ij}} }
by gradient descent, with

\frac{\partial C}{\partial y_i}
= 4\sum_{j}(p_{ij}-q_{ij}) (y_i-y_j) \big(1+\|y_i-y_j\|^2\big)^{-1}.

KL divergence is asymmetric, and that asymmetry defines t-SNE's
character. The cost of using a small $q_{ij}$ where $p_{ij}$ is large is
$p_{ij}\log\frac{p_{ij}}{q_{ij}}$ — huge. The cost of using a large $q_{ij}$
where $p_{ij}$ is small is nearly zero, because the $p_{ij}$ prefactor kills it.

So t-SNE is heavily penalised for separating true neighbours and barely
penalised for placing distant points near each other. It therefore
preserves local structure faithfully and global structure not at all. Every
misreading of a t-SNE plot traces back to this one equation.

Two implementation tricks make it work in practice. Early exaggeration
multiplies all $p_{ij}$ by 12 for the first 250 iterations, forcing tight
clusters to form early with lots of empty space between them, which prevents the
optimiser from getting stuck. Barnes–Hut approximation groups distant
points using a quad-tree, cutting the cost from $O(n^2)$ to $O(n\log n)$; this is
sklearn's default method="barnes_hut" and it restricts the output to 2 or
3 dimensions.
Perplexity

blocks.cap:
The same digits at five perplexities. Below about 5 the algorithm sees
only immediate neighbours and shatters real classes; above about 50 it averages
over too many and merges them.

blocks.t: Reading perplexity
Perplexity $\approx$ the number of neighbours each point "pays attention to".

items:
Too small (2–5): the map fragments into many small clumps, most
of which are artefacts.

Sweet spot (5–50): the range the original paper recommends. 30
is the sklearn default and a reasonable first try.

Too large ($>n/3$): the Gaussians cover the whole dataset,
local structure is averaged away, and clusters merge.

blocks.t:
Always run two or three perplexities. Structure that survives all of
them is real; structure that appears at only one is not.
How t-SNE plots are misread

blocks.cap: Four measured demonstrations of what a t-SNE plot cannot tell you.

blocks.t:
1. Cluster sizes are meaningless. t-SNE equalises density by
construction — each point's $\sigma_i$ adapts to its local scale. Panel three
shows two true clusters with standard deviations 0.4 and 4.0 drawn at
essentially the same size. You cannot infer variance, spread, or cluster
population from the area of a blob.

2. Distances between clusters are meaningless. Panel four has clusters
separated by true distances of 3 and 40, and the plot gives no hint of the
difference. The KL objective simply does not care where distant points end up.
Never say "cluster A is closer to B than to C" from a t-SNE plot.

3. Random noise produces apparent clusters. Panel two is 40-dimensional
i.i.d. Gaussian noise at perplexity 5, and it looks convincingly clumpy. Low
perplexity manufactures structure. Confirm any cluster you see with an actual
clustering algorithm on the original features.

4. Every run is different. t-SNE is stochastic and non-convex. Panel
one overlays two seeds of the same data — the layouts are unrelated. Set
init="pca" and a random_state for reproducibility, and never
compare two separately-fitted t-SNE plots to each other.

Never use t-SNE output as features for a model. There is no
transform() — the embedding is defined only for the points it was fit
on, so a new row cannot be projected. Adding a test point means refitting
everything, which changes all the coordinates. If you want a nonlinear
representation for downstream modelling, use PCA, an autoencoder, or UMAP
(which does have a transform).
t-SNE vs UMAP vs PCA

Always run PCA first. Reducing to 30–50 principal components before
t-SNE removes noise dimensions, makes distances more meaningful, and speeds
everything up by an order of magnitude. It is standard practice and is what the
original paper recommends.
Code

import numpy as np
from sklearn.manifold import TSNE
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.metrics import adjusted_rand_score
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

digits = load_digits()
X, y = digits.data, digits.target        # 1797 x 64

# ==================================================================
# 1. THE STANDARD PIPELINE: scale -> PCA -> t-SNE
# ==================================================================
Xs = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)
Xp = PCA(n_components=30, random_state=0).fit_transform(Xs)  # denoise + speed up
print("variance kept by 30 PCs:",
      round(PCA(30, random_state=0).fit(Xs).explained_variance_ratio_.sum(), 3))

emb = TSNE(
        n_components  = 2,
        perplexity    = 30,      # THE parameter. 5-50. ~ effective #neighbours
        early_exaggeration = 12, # inflate P for the first 250 iters
        learning_rate = "auto",  # = max(n/12/4, 50); do not leave at the old 200
        init          = "pca",   # far more stable than "random" -- use it always
        max_iter      = 1000,    # 250 minimum; 1000 is a safe default
        metric        = "euclidean",
        random_state  = 0,       # reproducibility -- t-SNE is stochastic
        method        = "barnes_hut",   # O(n log n); exact is O(n^2)
    ).fit_transform(Xp)

print("KL divergence at convergence:",
      round(TSNE(perplexity=30, init="pca", random_state=0).fit(Xp).kl_divergence_, 4))

plt.figure(figsize=(7, 6))
sc = plt.scatter(emb[:, 0], emb[:, 1], c=y, cmap="tab10", s=6)
plt.colorbar(sc); plt.title("t-SNE of digits")
# plt.savefig("tsne.png", dpi=150)

# ==================================================================
# 2. THERE IS NO transform()
# ==================================================================
t = TSNE(n_components=2, init="pca", random_state=0)
t.fit(Xp)
try:
    t.transform(Xp[:5])
except AttributeError as e:
    print("no transform:", type(e).__name__)
# The embedding exists ONLY for the fitted points. To place new data you must
# refit everything -- and every coordinate will change. This is why t-SNE
# output must never be used as model features.

# ==================================================================
# 3. THE INSTABILITY, MEASURED
# ==================================================================
runs = [TSNE(2, perplexity=30, init="random", random_state=s,
             max_iter=500).fit_transform(Xp[:500]) for s in range(3)]
# The layouts differ completely, but the CLUSTER STRUCTURE is stable:
for i, e in enumerate(runs):
    lab = KMeans(10, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit_predict(e)
    print(f"seed {i}: ARI vs true labels = {adjusted_rand_score(y[:500], lab):.3f}")
# Same ARI, different pictures. Judge t-SNE by what groups together,
# never by where things sit.

# ==================================================================
# 4. SWEEPING PERPLEXITY -- always do this
# ==================================================================
for p in (5, 30, 50, 100):
    e = TSNE(2, perplexity=p, init="pca", random_state=0, max_iter=500).fit_transform(Xp)
    lab = KMeans(10, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit_predict(e)
    print(f"perplexity {p:3d}: ARI {adjusted_rand_score(y, lab):.3f}")
# Structure that survives every perplexity is real. Structure that appears at
# only one value is an artefact of that bandwidth.

# ==================================================================
# 5. WHAT NOT TO DO
# ==================================================================
# WRONG -- t-SNE coordinates as features for a classifier:
#   emb = TSNE(2).fit_transform(X_train)
#   clf.fit(emb, y_train)          # cannot ever score X_test
#
# WRONG -- fitting train and test separately and comparing the plots:
#   e1 = TSNE(2).fit_transform(X_train)
#   e2 = TSNE(2).fit_transform(X_test)   # unrelated coordinate systems
#
# WRONG -- measuring the gap between two clusters in the plot.
#
# RIGHT -- t-SNE to LOOK at the data; PCA/UMAP/autoencoder to MODEL it.

# ==================================================================
# 6. UMAP -- the modern alternative (pip install umap-learn)
# ==================================================================
# import umap
# reducer = umap.UMAP(n_neighbors=15,    # analogous to perplexity
#                     min_dist=0.1,      # how tightly points may pack
#                     n_components=2,
#                     random_state=0)
# emb_train = reducer.fit_transform(Xp)
# emb_test  = reducer.transform(Xp_new)   # <-- t-SNE cannot do this
#
# UMAP is faster, keeps more global structure, and supports transform(), so it
# can (carefully) be used as a preprocessing step as well as for plotting.

# ==================================================================
# 7. VALIDATING WHAT YOU SEE
# ==================================================================
# Never trust a cluster you only saw in a t-SNE plot. Confirm it by clustering
# the ORIGINAL features and checking the groups agree.
lab_hi = KMeans(10, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit_predict(Xp)     # original space
lab_lo = KMeans(10, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit_predict(emb)    # t-SNE space
print("agreement between spaces:", round(adjusted_rand_score(lab_hi, lab_lo), 3))
Everything on one page
Summary

Idea: convert distances to neighbour probabilities in high-D ($P$,
Gaussian with a per-point $\sigma_i$) and in 2-D ($Q$, Student-t with 1 dof),
then move the 2-D points to minimise $\mathrm{KL}(P\|Q)$.

Perplexity $=2^{H(P_i)}$ sets the effective number of neighbours and
fixes each $\sigma_i$ by binary search. Range 5–50; sweep it.

The Student-t solves the crowding problem: its heavy tail creates the
room that 2-D lacks for the many moderately-distant points of a
high-dimensional space.

KL is asymmetric, so t-SNE is punished for splitting true neighbours
but not for merging distant points. Hence: local structure is trustworthy,
global structure is not.

Four things a t-SNE plot cannot tell you: cluster size, distance
between clusters, whether apparent clusters are real (noise makes them), or
anything reproducible across runs.

Always: scale, PCA to 30–50 components first, init="pca", set
random_state, run several perplexities, and confirm clusters in the
original space.

Never: use the coordinates as model features — there is no
transform().
Interview corner
Q. How does t-SNE differ from PCA?

PCA is a linear projection maximising retained variance; it preserves global
structure, is deterministic, invertible, and has a transform for new
data. t-SNE is a non-linear, stochastic optimisation that preserves local
neighbourhoods only, has no transform, and produces a different picture
every run. PCA is for modelling; t-SNE is for looking.
Q. What is perplexity?

$2^{H(P_i)}$ — a smooth measure of the effective number of neighbours each
point considers. It determines each point's Gaussian bandwidth $\sigma_i$ via
binary search, adaptively: small in dense regions, large in sparse ones.
Q. Why the Student-t distribution in the low-dimensional space?

To fix the crowding problem. High-dimensional space has far more room at
moderate distances than 2-D does, so those points would be crushed together.
The t-distribution's heavy tail means a given similarity corresponds to a larger
map distance, creating the extra space and letting clusters separate.
Q. Why is KL divergence used, and why does its asymmetry matter?

$\mathrm{KL}(P\|Q)=\sum p\log(p/q)$ heavily penalises small $q$ where $p$ is
large — pulling true neighbours apart — but barely penalises large $q$ where
$p$ is small. So t-SNE guards local structure and ignores global structure. That
single fact explains every caveat about reading the plots.
Q. Can you interpret the distance between two clusters?

No. The objective assigns almost no cost to where distant points land. Clusters
that are far apart in the original space may be drawn adjacent and vice versa.
Only "these points are neighbours" is trustworthy.
Q. Can you interpret cluster sizes?

No. The adaptive per-point bandwidth equalises density, so a tight cluster and a
diffuse one are drawn at similar sizes.
Q. Why can't you use t-SNE for feature engineering?

It has no out-of-sample extension — the embedding is defined only for the
fitted points, so test data cannot be projected without refitting, and refitting
changes every coordinate. Use PCA, an autoencoder, or UMAP instead.
Q. What is early exaggeration?

Multiplying all $p_{ij}$ by a factor (12 by default) for the first few hundred
iterations. It makes clusters form tightly with wide gaps between them early on,
which helps the non-convex optimisation avoid poor local minima.
Q. Why run PCA before t-SNE?

It removes noise dimensions so that Euclidean distances are more meaningful,
and it reduces the cost of the neighbour computation by an order of magnitude.
30–50 components is standard.
Q. When would you use UMAP instead?

When you need speed on large datasets, want more of the global structure
preserved, or need a transform for new points. UMAP is generally the
better default now; t-SNE remains the better-understood reference, and their
local structure usually agrees.
Worked Examples
Turning distances into neighbour probabilities
Three points on a line: $x = [0,\;1,\;3]$. t-SNE converts distances into conditional probabilities with a Gaussian of width $\sigma = 1$:
p_{j\mid i} = \frac{\exp \big(-\|x_i-x_j\|^2/2\sigma^2\big)}{\sum_{k\ne i}\exp \big(-\|x_i-x_k\|^2/2\sigma^2\big)}
From point 0.
Almost all of point 0's probability mass sits on its near neighbour. That is the point of the method: local neighbourhoods are preserved.
Symmetrise. $p_{ij} = \dfrac{p_{j\mid i}+p_{i\mid j}}{2n}$, so each pair gets one joint probability.
Low-dimensional map. The embedding uses a heavy-tailed Student-t kernel $q_{ij} \propto (1+\|y_i-y_j\|^2)^{-1}$, which lets distant points spread apart and avoids the crowding problem.
Warning. The perplexity parameter sets the effective $\sigma$ for each point. The layout depends on it, and cluster sizes and gaps in a t-SNE picture are not quantitatively meaningful.
